<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

</document>
response:
# Review of Achterberg et al., "Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis"

This is the most useful of the four documents. It asks the right questions: it separates per-hour from per-worker output, codes work type, prefers actual hours, excludes self-rated productivity, reports a prediction interval, and checks for small-study bias. Its central conclusion seems sound:

- the per-hour gain is real but much smaller than headline pilots suggest;
- output per worker falls clearly in coverage-bound work;
- neither "sector-general" nor "entirely an artifact" is supported.

The main problems are:

- two strong claims that the analyses cannot carry: that effects show no decay, and that the small-study asymmetry reflects publication bias;
- an abstract that reports a less rigorous per-worker figure than the paper itself prefers;
- unclear handling of the two studies this series has examined closely.

## Arithmetic and internal consistency

The reported intervals are consistent on the log scale:

- the pooled per-hour estimate of +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0);
- the trim-and-fill estimate of +9.1% (3.9 to 14.6);
- the controlled estimate of +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6);
- the coverage-bound per-worker estimate of −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5);
- the prediction interval of −4% to +34%, which implies τ ≈ 0.08, consistent with I² = 81%.

The per-hour and per-worker subgroup figures also imply plausible hours reductions, between about 11% and 15%. I found no numerical errors.

---

## Strengths

- **The moderators are the right ones**, and the paper is candid that design and measurement are confounded (12 of 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours).
- **The restricted analysis of controlled discretionary studies** (+9.6% per hour, −2.7% per worker) is exactly the figure decision-makers need, and the paper volunteers it.
- **The prediction interval is reported and interpreted correctly.** Many meta-analyses omit this.
- **The fatigue result is informative.** The weak correlation between fatigue improvement and per-hour gain (r = 0.18) cuts against the explanation Halden favoured. It deserves more prominence than it gets.
- **The rebuttal of both extremes** ("sector-general" and "entirely an artifact") is, on balance, correct.

---

## Problems

### 1. "No sign of decay" is not supported

This claim appears in both the abstract and the Duration section ("novelty explanations can therefore be set aside"). It rests on comparing four studies with more than 12 months' follow-up against the rest. That is a weak basis:

- **It compares studies, not time points.** Studies with long follow-up differ from short ones in setting, design and who ran them. Decay would show up in how effects change over time *within* studies, and that is not examined.
- **It suffers from survivorship.** Schemes that disappoint are typically ended or not written up beyond the pilot. Long-follow-up studies are therefore likely to be the successes.
- **Four studies give little power.** The interval of +6.2% to +22.4% is wide. "Indistinguishable from the overall estimate" means absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.

Varga & Holm's novelty argument was itself weak: it rested on an energy proxy and an untested extrapolation. But this analysis does not refute it. The authors should:

- extract within-study trajectories where studies report output at several time points;
- report the design and measurement characteristics of the four long studies;
- downgrade the abstract wording to "durability is unresolved". Median follow-up is 6 months.

### 2. The funnel asymmetry may reflect design, not publication bias

The small studies are probably the uncontrolled, scheduled-hours, manager-reported pilots, and those features are already known to produce larger estimates. Under these conditions:

- Egger's test and trim-and-fill are unreliable when heterogeneity is high (I² = 81%) and moderators correlate with study size.
- The asymmetry is equally consistent with "small studies are worse-designed", and those explanations have different implications.

The authors should run the asymmetry test with the design and measurement moderators included, or within the controlled subgroup alone. The interpretation should then be framed as "small-study effects" rather than publication bias specifically. The trim-and-fill figure of 9.1% should not be counted as independent support for the 8–10% range (see point 4).

### 3. The abstract reports the weaker per-worker figure for discretionary work

The abstract says output per worker fell in coverage-bound work "but not in discretionary (+0.6%)". That +0.6% mixes in uncontrolled studies. The paper's own controlled-only figure is −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2). The pooled controlled per-worker estimate of −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5), whose interval excludes zero, appears nowhere in the abstract.

The Discussion handles this correctly ("maintained or falling slightly"). The abstract should match it, because most readers will read only the abstract.

### 4. The "convergence" on 8–10% is one set of studies seen four times

The Discussion says that four lines of evidence converge on a gain of roughly 8–10%:

- controlled studies (8.2%);
- actual-hours studies (7.9%);
- record-based studies (9.7%);
- the bias-adjusted estimate (9.1%).

These are not independent. The controlled studies are probably largely the same studies that measured actual hours and used records. The paper should report the cell that matters, **controlled + actual hours + record-based output**, with its k. It should also report the **three randomised trials** separately. Only those directly address the selection and measurement problems Varga & Holm raised, because "matched or difference-in-differences" designs do not remove selection.

### 5. Varden and Halden may be miscoded or mishandled

**Work-type coding.** Both studies contain discretionary and coverage-bound work:

- Varden's two strata are reported separately.
- Halden includes retail and hospitality.

Yet the counts (13 + 7 + 3 = 23) mean each study sits in one category. The "mixed" category has three studies, two of which are manufacturing. So at most one of Halden and Varden was coded "mixed", and the other must have been forced into a single category despite containing both types. Varden's strata are pre-specified, separately estimated results. They should enter as two effect sizes, with the dependence handled through robust variance estimation or a multilevel model, and Halden should likewise be split by sector.

**The Halden data.** The paper doesn't say whether it used the figures as originally reported, or Varga & Holm's corrected microdata (actual hours for 27 organisations, records for 23). Given the stated preference for actual hours, the corrected figures seem appropriate. The attrition misdescription also bears on Halden's risk of bias.

### 6. There is no risk-of-bias assessment

The review codes design and measurement as moderators, but does not apply a structured tool such as ROBINS-I, RoB 2 or GRADE. As a result, attrition, the independence of outcome assessors, and selective reporting are never assessed. Halden's attrition problem, nine withdrawals mostly after the schedule began, would be invisible to this review. A risk-of-bias table is standard and should be added.

### 7. Subgroup comparisons lack formal tests, and the meta-regression is fragile

- **No formal tests.** Subgroup differences are described without tests for between-group differences. Several intervals overlap substantially, such as actual hours (3.6 to 12.4) versus scheduled hours (9.9 to 23.7).
- **Fragile meta-regression.** It has k = 23 and three collinear moderators, and reports no coefficients. The "58% of variance explained" figure is likely unstable.

The Limitations section acknowledges the small base. The authors should still report the tests and coefficients and treat them as exploratory.

### 8. Coverage-bound per-hour gains need interpretation

The paper calls the +6.2% coverage-bound per-hour gain "real but too small to compensate". As I noted on Varden, in queue-based work fewer staff means less idle time between customers. Output per hour then rises because the public waits longer, not because staff work better.

The review should say this outright. It should also code service-quality outcomes (waiting times, abandonment) wherever studies report them. In addition, "consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%)" overstates what a small k can show, since I² estimated from seven studies is very imprecise.

### 9. Smaller points

- **Sick leave.** The pooled −31% has the same mechanical issue I raised for both trials: fewer scheduled days leave fewer days on which to be absent. Code sick leave per scheduled day where possible. "Fell in all 14" is vote-counting and should be supplemented by a pooled estimate with an interval.
- **Different estimands pooled.** The overall estimate combines difference-in-differences estimates with uncontrolled before–after changes, which absorb secular trends. Lead with the controlled estimate and present the all-studies pool as descriptive.
- **Manager-reported output.** This is included even though self-rated productivity was excluded, and Varga & Holm showed it overstates output by about 4 points. The record-based row is the right sensitivity check and should feature more prominently.
- **Cost implications.** The Discussion notes that coverage-bound settings "would require additional staff" to maintain service. Saying roughly how much would help: about 10% more staff at full pay, given a 9% per-worker fall.

---

## Suggested revisions

1. Replace "no sign of decay" with an analysis of within-study trajectories, or state that durability is unresolved.
2. Re-run the small-study tests with moderators included, and describe the result as "small-study effects".
3. Correct the abstract to report the controlled per-worker figures.
4. Report the controlled + actual-hours + record-based cell, and the randomised trials separately.
5. Enter Varden's strata, and Halden by sector, as separate effect sizes. State which version of the Halden data was used.
6. Add a risk-of-bias assessment that includes attrition.
7. Add formal subgroup tests and meta-regression coefficients.
8. Interpret coverage-bound per-hour gains as partly a utilisation effect, and code service-quality outcomes.

---

## Where the four documents leave the evidence

| Question | Best current answer | Main basis |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | Roughly 8–12%, credibly above zero | Varden case-processing; controlled subgroup |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Unchanged to slightly lower (about 0 to −3%) | Varden; controlled discretionary studies |
| Per-worker output, coverage-bound work | About 9–11% lower, with worse service | Varden counters; meta-analysis subgroup |
| Halden's 23.4% | Substantially overstated: about 11% after partial correction, attrition uncorrected | Varga & Holm |
| "Sector-general" | Not supported | All three critiques |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported | Randomised and controlled evidence |
| Durability beyond about 9 months | Unresolved | No adequate within-study evidence |
| Mechanism | Fatigue is weakly supported; meetings are plausible but untested | Meta-analysis r = 0.18; Varden exploratory analysis |
| Cost per unit of output | Largely unreported | Gap in all four documents |

The questions that most need new evidence are durability, mechanism (especially whether the gains could be had by cutting meetings without cutting hours), and cost. Varden's registered 24-month follow-up is the study best placed to answer the first two. I can turn this into a short briefing note or a referee report for any of the four papers if that would help.
